full results appear in \\\\S\\\\ref{sec:experiments}.\\n\\n\\\\paragraph{Pitfall 1: Method sensitivity.}\\nApplied to the same data ($\\\\alpha{=}1.0$, 4~seeds, 16 canary$\\\\to$downstream pairs: 4 candidate canaries $\\\\times$ 4 downstream metrics, including candidates later excluded per \\\\S\\\\ref{sec:case_study}), five lead-lag detection methods yield FDR significance rates ranging from 100\\\\% (naive cross-correlation) to 25\\\\% (Toda--Yamamoto Granger causality), with inter-method agreement of Cohen's $\\\\kappa{=}0.185$, indicating poor agreement (\\\\S\\\\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}).\\nThe spurious-signal rate (the fraction of pairs flagged by the most liberal method but not confirmed by the most conservative) is 75\\\\% across all five methods and 62.5\\\\% when excluding Toda--Yamamoto, whose low statistical power at $T{=}10$ inflates this rate.\\nThis pitfall is dangerous because method choice alone can determine whether a lead-lag relationship is deemed present or absent.\\nIn a literature where single-method analyses are the norm, the implicit assumption that method choice does not matter is demonstrably false.\\n\\n\\\\paragraph{Pitfall 2: Spurious regression under shared trends.}\\nA single preprocessing decision, first-differencing to remove shared non-stationary trends~\\\\cite{granger1974spurious}, can eliminate an entire analysis channel.\\nAt $\\\\alpha{=}1.0$, canary$\\\\to$perplexity pairs appear near-universally significant in undifferenced analysis ($F{=}16$--$36$) but yield $F{\\\\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$ after differencing (Figure~\\\\ref{fig:differencing_dmax}a; \\\\S\\\\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}).\\nIn contrast, canary$\\\\to$diversity pairs retain unanimous FDR significance after differencing (24/24$\\\\to$24/24).\\nWithout the differencing diagnostic, an analyst would conclude that canaries predict perplexity, a conclusion entirely driven by co-trending rather than temporal precedence.\\nThe danger lies in the selective nature of this confound: only by applying the diagnostic can one determine which channels are genuine and which are artifacts of shared non-stationarity.\\n\\n\\\\paragraph{Pitfall 3: Regime dependence.}\\nEven after fixing the statistical method, the contamination level~$\\\\alpha$ determines whether a lead-lag relationship is detectable.\\nPermutation Granger tests (first-differenced, BH FDR-corrected at $q{=}0.05$) find 6/8 pairs FDR-significant at $\\\\alpha{=}1.0$ but 0/24 at $\\\\alpha{\\\\leq}0.25$ (three seeds), with seed-dependent results (0/8--6/8) at $\\\\alpha{=}0.50$ (\\\\S\\\\ref{sec:regime}).\\nThe $\\\\alpha{=}0.50$ regime is particularly dangerous: for seed~42, correlation-based methods unanimously find significance while causal methods find non-significance (Figure~\\\\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap}); for other seeds, partial Granger significance emerges (3/8 and 6/8), illustrating seed-dependent divergence at this boundary and creating the maximum risk of spurious conclusions when only a single seed is analyzed.\\nThis regime dependence is consistent with theoretical expectations about signal-to-noise limits in short ecological time series \\\\cite{boettiger2012limits}, and suggests that detectability boundaries should be explicitly mapped rather than assumed.\\n\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Multi-Method Consensus Framework}\\n\\\\label{sec:consensus}\\n\\nThe pitfalls above motivate a consensus approach inspired by multi-method validation practices in early-warning signal detection \\\\cite{scheffer2009early}: rather than relying on any single method, we require agreement across multiple independent methods and random seeds before classifying a lead-lag relationship as robust.\\n\\n\\\\paragraph{Formal definition.}\\nGiven $M$ lead-lag detection methods $\\\\{m_1, \\\\ldots, m_M\\\\}$ and $N$ independent random seeds, a canary$\\\\to$downstream pair $(X, Y)$ is classified as \\\\textsc{robust} if and only if:\\n\\\\begin{enumerate}\\n    \\\\item At least $K$ of $M$ methods judge the pair FDR-significant, where each method independently applies Benjamini--Hochberg correction at $q{=}0.05$; and\\n    \\\\item At least $S$ of $N$ seeds replicate this conclusion.\\n\\\\end{enumerate}\\nThe thresholds $(K, S)$ control the trade-off between false positive and false negative rates.\\nMethods with different inductive biases (correlation-based methods that detect any temporal association versus Granger-type methods that test directional predictive improvement \\\\cite{granger1969investigating}) provide complementary evidence.\\nTheir convergence on a given pair constitutes stronger evidence than agreement among methods sharing the same statistical assumptions.\\nWe note that Granger precedence establishes temporal predictive improvement, not true causality \\\\cite{shojaie2022granger}; our framework inherits this limitation.\\n\\n\\\\paragraph{Sequential filtering pipeline.}\\nIn practice, the $K$-of-$M$ voting operates over all five methods applied independently to each pair; the sequential pipeline below describes the order in which results are examined, enabling early termination and interpretable diagnostics at each stage (Figure~\\\\ref{fig:consensus_workflow}):\\n\\\\begin{enumerate}\\n    \\\\item \\\\textbf{Naive correlation scan.} Cross-correlation at maximum lag~5 with BH correction serves as a permissive baseline; all pairs with any temporal association pass.\\n    \\\\item \\\\textbf{First-differencing diagnostic.} Cross-correlation is recomputed on first-differenced series, testing whether temporal associations survive removal of shared linear trends. Pairs that lose significance are flagged as potential spurious regressions.\\n    \\\\item \\\\textbf{Permutation Granger causality.} Permutation-based Granger causality tests \\\\cite{shojaie2022granger} on first-differenced series (5{,}000 permutations, BH correction at $q{=}0.05$) assess directional predictive improvement: whether past values of $X$ improve prediction of $Y$ beyond $Y$'s own history.\\n    \\\\item \\\\textbf{Multi-seed replication.} The conclusion must hold across $S$ of $N$ independent training seeds, filtering seed-specific artifacts.\\n\\\\end{enumerate}\\nAt $\\\\alpha{=}1.0$, this pipeline progressively filters: 16 pairs pass Stage~1, 14 survive Stage~2 (differencing removes 2 marginal canary$\\\\to$perplexity pairs), 6 survive Stage~3 (Granger testing eliminates remaining canary$\\\\to$perplexity pairs and failed canary candidates), and all~6 survive Stage~4 (multi-seed replication confirms all Granger-significant pairs).\\n\\n\\\\begin{figure}[t]\\n\", \"stderr\": \"\", \"return_code\": 0}, \"error\": null, \"metadata\": {\"elapsed_seconds\": 0.44}}"}

{"success": true, "data": {"stdout": "\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Practitioners monitoring iterative training pipelines face a diagnostic blind spot: the metrics most commonly used to detect distributional degradation can yield false positive rates of 62.5--100\% when applied without proper statistical controls, yet no established protocol exists for distinguishing genuine early-warning signals from artifacts of shared non-stationary trends.
This blind spot is consequential because iterative training collapse, where models are unwittingly trained on output from earlier generations, is increasingly likely as machine-generated text proliferates on the web~\cite{shumailov2024curse,alemohammad2024mad}.
Tail modes vanish, lexical diversity narrows, and calibration deteriorates across generations.
These failure modes motivate the search for cheap-to-compute \emph{canary metrics} that provide early warning, analogous to early-warning signals for critical transitions in ecological and climate systems~\cite{scheffer2009early,scheffer2012anticipating}.

Several recent studies have pursued this direction: \citet{du2026geometric} informally observe that expected calibration error rises before accuracy degrades; SIGMA~\cite{sigma2026spectral} proposes spectral indicators of distributional shift; and DCES~\cite{dces2026counter} uses center-edge sampling dynamics as a collapse signal.
Yet the statistical methodology underlying these lead-lag claims (whether a canary metric genuinely \emph{precedes} downstream degradation, or merely correlates with it under shared non-stationary trends) has received little scrutiny.

We identify several methodological deficiencies that pervade existing lead-lag analyses of iterative training collapse:
(1)~no differencing tests to rule out spurious regression arising from shared non-stationary trends, a well-known hazard when correlating co-trending time series;
(2)~no multi-method cross-validation; conclusions rest on a single statistical method whose implicit assumptions about stationarity and directionality are rarely examined;
(3)~no multiple comparison correction (e.g., Benjamini--Hochberg FDR control), increasing the risk of false discoveries when testing many metric pairs simultaneously; and
(4)~no regime-dependent analysis, despite the possibility that the same statistical test yields opposite conclusions at different contamination levels.
The closest predecessor is \citet{du2026geometric}, who observe that calibration error rises before accuracy degrades in iteratively trained language models.
Their analysis, however, is limited to a single metric pair, spans only 1--3 generations, and reports informal visual comparisons without statistical tests, leaving open the question of whether the observed lead is genuine or an artifact of shared trends.
The early-warning framework of \citet{scheffer2009early,scheffer2012anticipating}, widely adopted in ecology for anticipating tipping points, provides the theoretical motivation for canary-based prediction, but has not been systematically applied to iterative training collapse with the methodological rigor that short, noisy time series demand~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.

\subsection{Cross-Architecture, Cross-Scale, and Cross-Domain Generalization}
\label{sec:generalization}

The methodological pitfalls and consensus framework developed above are calibrated on a single model family (Pythia-410M, WikiText-103).
To test whether these findings transfer, we evaluate the consensus pipeline along three generalization axes: architecture family (GPT-2-medium 345M, OPT-1.3B), model scale (Pythia-1.4B, $3.4\times$ parameters within the same family), and training domain (Pythia-1B trained on C4 rather than WikiText-103).
All conditions use $\alpha{=}1.0$ and a single seed.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Generalization of lead-lag detectability across architecture, scale, and domain ($\alpha{=}1.0$, single seed per condition). Each cell reports the fraction of canary$\to$downstream pairs reaching BH-corrected FDR significance ($q{=}0.05$): 8~pairs for Pythia models and OPT-1.3B, 6~pairs for GPT-2-medium (MAUVE excluded). }
\label{tab:generalization}
\begin{tabular}{llccccccc}
\toprule
Variation & Model / Dataset & \rotatebox{70}{Naive} & \rotatebox{70}{Diff.\ XCorr} & \rotatebox{70}{Threshold} & \rotatebox{70}{PermG (fwd)} & \rotatebox{70}{PermG (rev)} & \rotatebox{70}{TY} & \rotatebox{70}{$K{\geq}4/5$} \\
\midrule
Baseline      & Pythia-410M / Wiki    & 7/8 & 6/8 & 6/8 & 6/8 & 0/8 & 6/8 & 6/8 \\
Architecture  & GPT-2-medium / Wiki   & 6/6 & 6/6 & 6/6 & 6/6 & 0/6 & 0/6 & 6/6 \\
Architecture  & OPT-1.3B / Wiki       & 6/8 & 6/8 & 8/8 & 6/8 & 0/8 & 2/8 & 6/8 \\
Scale ($3.4\times$) & Pythia-1.4B / Wiki    & 7/8 & 6/8 & 8/8 & 5/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 & 5/8 \\
Domain        & Pythia-1B / C4        & 7/8 & 8/8 & 8/8 & 8/8 & 3/8 & 4/8 & 8/8$^\dagger$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\vspace{2pt}
{\footnotesize $^\dagger$C4 domain: token\_entropy pairs maintain strict unidirectionality (rev=0/4); ECE pairs show bidirectional coupling (rev=3/4), reflecting canary-specific signal quality differences across domains.}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Architecture generalization.}
Table~\ref{tab:generalization} confirms that the entropy-leads-diversity pattern generalizes across all three decoder-only transformer families tested to date.
All models reach Tier~3 consensus ($K{\geq}4/5$) with 6/8 (or 6/6) canary$\to$diversity pairs confirmed.
Permutation Granger directionality is perfect across architectures: all forward-direction pairs are FDR-significant while 0 reverse-direction pairs reach significance in any architecture.

Method-level variation across architectures is informative.
Threshold onset detection reaches 8/8 on OPT-1.3B (the highest single-method score) because OPT's token entropy exhibits a pronounced generation-0$\to$1 discontinuity that cleanly exceeds the onset threshold.
Toda--Yamamoto ranges from 0/6 (GPT-2-medium) to 6/8 (Pythia-410M), consistent with its known sensitivity to residual degrees of freedom at short series lengths (\S\ref{sec:consensus_validation}).
Despite this cross-method variance, the consensus threshold absorbs it: all three architectures converge at $K{\geq}4/5$.

\paragraph{Scale generalization.}
Pythia-1.4B (3.4$\times$ parameters relative to the 410M baseline) maintains $K{\geq}4/5$ with 5/8 consensus pairs, confirming that the lead-lag signal persists across model scale.
Permutation Granger reverse significance is 0/8, preserving perfect directionality at the larger scale.
The modest decrease from 6/8 to 5/8 reflects two token\_entropy pairs (\textrightarrow perplexity, \textrightarrow distinct\_3) falling below threshold, likely due to higher perplexity variance in the 1.4B model.
Toda--Yamamoto yields 0/8 significant pairs, consistent with GPT-2-medium results and attributable to insufficient residual degrees of freedom at short series length ($T{=}10$) rather than method failure.

\paragraph{Domain generalization.}
Replacing WikiText-103 with C4 tests whether the lead-lag pattern depends on the training data distribution.
We exclude perplexity as a downstream variable in the C4 setting: its exponential divergence (20.6$\to$1682.6, ADF statistic $+1.07$) violates the stationarity assumption required by VAR-based Granger analysis.
Instead, we use bounded diversity metrics (distinct-$n$, MAUVE) which remain well-behaved under differencing.

Table~\ref{tab:generalization} shows that Pythia-1B on C4 achieves 8/8 consensus at $K{\geq}4/5$, exceeding the Tier~3 threshold established by the WikiText baseline (6/8).
Permutation Granger forward detection reaches 8/8, the strongest single-method score across all generalization conditions.
